summary: Describes how to manage early media in SIP using a gateway model and an application server model. It also lists the inputs to consider in setting local policy for generating ringing tones.

eli5.summary: Before somebody answers a phone, you may hear a ringing sound or a recorded message. This memo explains who should play it and how.

questions: how to manage early media in sip
what is media clipping and how to avoid it
when should local ringing be generated
how does sip handle call forking with early media
subtitle: Managing audio and video before a call is accepted.

tldr.problem: In VoIP with SIP, early media (ringing tones or announcements) plays before the called party answers, but SIP's basic mechanisms for managing this create problems with forking and media clipping (losing the start of audio).
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3960 describes two models: a gateway model (simpler but with limitations) and an application server model (more robust) that separate early media from regular media sessions and use the offer/answer negotiation model cleanly.
tldr.outcome: SIP implementations can now manage early media reliably, let callers hear ringing or recorded messages without losing audio at the start, and handle call forwarding without cutting off media streams.

facts.label: Recommended local ringing policy
facts.value: Play if 180 received and no media packets arrive

facts.label: Key limitation of gateway model
facts.value: Media clipping and ambiguity with call forking

today: RFC 3960 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It describes two approaches for managing early media in SIP implementations. The application server model (using RFC 3959) is the recommended approach for robust early media handling in modern SIP deployments.

sections.title: The Early Media Problem
sections.content:
Early media is audio or video exchanged before the called user accepts the call – ringing tones, announcements like "Your call is being connected" or IVR prompts. The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) lets endpoints negotiate and exchange media using the offer/answer model, but the basic specification has limitations for early media.

The core challenge is deciding who should play ringing tones when the call is forwarded to multiple destinations (forking). Another challenge is media clipping – losing the first few words when switching from local ringing to incoming audio. Without clear rules, endpoints make different decisions, creating poor user experience.

This document defines two implementation models to handle early media cleanly. Both are more sophisticated than the approach in the base SIP specification (RFC 3261) and address real deployment scenarios.
sections.eli5: When someone forwards your call to three people at once, the caller hears ringing, but which phone generates that ringing tone? If someone answers, the caller should hear them, not the local ringing. Keeping that switch smooth is the problem this memo solves.

sections.title: SIP Session Establishment Basics
sections.content:
SIP uses an offer/answer model where one endpoint (the offerer) sends a session description, and the other (the answerer) responds with a compatible description. This two-way handshake negotiates media parameters before sending any media packets.

The timing of this exchange matters. When an INVITE (call initiation) carries an offer and a 200 OK response carries the answer, endpoints are ready to exchange media as soon as the offer is sent. But if the answer comes in the ACK (acknowledgment), media clipping becomes unavoidable – the answerer begins speaking when sending the 200 OK, but cannot send media until the UAC (caller) receives the offer and sends the ACK back.

Early media sessions (offer/answer exchanges before a final response) let provisional responses (like 180 Ringing) carry session descriptions. This avoids media clipping when used correctly.
sections.eli5: Before sending media, caller and receiver must agree on audio format. The timing of this agreement – before the call starts or just as it starts – affects whether the first words get lost.

sections.title: The Gateway Model and Its Limitations
sections.content:
The gateway model manages early media by exchanging offers and answers in reliable provisional responses, PRACK messages, and UPDATE requests – all within a single early dialog between the original INVITE and a final response.

This model works for simple non-forking scenarios. The calling endpoint gets a 180 Ringing response with an answer, can play early audio, and then transitions to regular media when the 200 OK arrives.

However, the gateway model fails with forking. When one INVITE reaches multiple destinations and several send provisional responses with different answers, the caller receives conflicting offers. The caller can only accept one early media session but receives media from multiple sources. If the caller mutes some sessions and one of those subsequently sends a 200 OK, media clipping occurs because the caller must unmute it with a new offer, and the answering endpoint cannot send media until receiving that offer.

Another limitation is deciding when to play local ringing versus expecting incoming media. A caller cannot easily tell whether a UAS intends to send early media just from SIP messages – it must detect incoming packets or rely on explicit indicators. The memo recommends the gateway model only when the endpoint cannot distinguish early from regular media (such as a PSTN gateway receiving circuit audio).
sections.eli5: The gateway model works when calling one person but breaks when the call rings multiple phones. If one person answers while another was muted, the caller loses the first words of that person's voice.

sections.title: The Application Server Model
sections.content:
The application server model addresses gateway model limitations by treating early media as a separate service. The endpoint indicates support for the early-session disposition type (defined in RFC 3959) using an option tag.

Under this model, early media uses a completely separate offer/answer exchange and dialog from the one carrying regular media. The caller can reject or mute offers for early media without affecting the dialog that will eventually carry the conversation. This lets the caller prioritize media correctly: discard or mute early media sessions from non-winning call branches, then smoothly transition to regular media when one endpoint answers.

Because early media is a distinct session, the caller can also make clearer decisions about local ringing. If a new early session containing audio arrives, the caller knows early media is coming and should suppress local ringing. The application server model is recommended for most deployments and handles both forking and ringing generation cleanly.

When a UA receives an early session offer carrying audio, it can immediately assume incoming early media is on the way and stop generating local ringing tone.
sections.eli5: Instead of using one conversation for both ringing and talking, use two separate conversations: one for ringing and messages (which you can discard), one for the real call. If one person answers, drop the ringing conversation and use the real conversation.

sections.title: Ringing Tone Generation and Policy
sections.content:
The memo defines a local ringing tone generation policy for POTS (Plain Old Telephone Service) style endpoints: (1) never generate local ringing unless a 180 Ringing response is received, (2) if 180 Ringing is received but no media packets arrive, play local ringing, (3) if 180 Ringing is received and media packets arrive, play the incoming media and stop local ringing.

This policy is achievable with tools already required by SIP (media clipping avoidance). Unlike some signaling protocols, SIP does not include an explicit early media indicator. Such an indicator would be of limited value anyway because media and signaling traverse different network paths – media often arrives before SIP messages indicating early media. Instead, endpoints should detect incoming packets directly.

The Alert-Info header field allows specifying an alternative ringing tone or alert content, but it does not tell the endpoint whether to generate local ringing. It merely provides guidance on what to play if the endpoint decides to generate ringing. The decision to ring locally follows the policy above, regardless of Alert-Info.
sections.eli5: Play local ringing only if asked (180 response), and stop it immediately when real audio arrives. Use Alert-Info to choose what kind of ringing to play locally, not to decide whether to play it.

left.title: Gateway Model
left.desc: Early media and regular media in one dialog. Fails with forking.

right.title: Application Server Model
right.desc: Early media in separate session. Clean handling of forking.

messages.label: Early media (audio)
messages.note: Caller stops local ringing, plays incoming audio
